title: Hymn and Winter
premise: Mara Vane hosts the overnight show 'Hymn and Winter' from a studio in the dying village of Coldharbour, where callers begin phoning in — people who died the previous week, all asking her to pass messages to their families before the church bell finishes ringing. The bell was melted down in 1911, but its tolling marks a count: when it reaches one hundred, everyone who has ever ignored a message from the dead will be collected. Mara, who spent twelve years rationalizing the voices she inherited from her grandmother's radio, must finally believe, gather the village's grieving families, and deliver every undelivered message before the hundredth ring — even though the last message is addressed to her. In the end, Mara answers her own call, breaking the inheritance of silence that doomed Coldharbour's founders, and the bell falls silent mid-count with ninety-nine rung.
about_author: Theo Fairweather is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years answering calls from insomniacs, grief-stricken strangers, and at least one voice he could never explain. He writes horror about small communities, old machines, and the things we agree not to hear.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. During her overnight broadcast, a caller named Edith praises the weather — then mentions her own funeral last Tuesday. Mara checks the log; the number is disconnected, the timestamp impossible. She tells herself it's a prank, but her hands shake through the sign-off. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional calm, the first crack in twelve years of denial.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. At dawn the church bell rings — the bell melted down in 1911, whose empty tower stands over Coldharbour like a pulled tooth. Old Mr. Halloway crosses himself; children film it on phones. Mara finds her grandmother's old receiver in the attic, warm despite the cold. Emotional beat: the past asserting itself, inheritance becoming undeniable.

chapters.title: Messages Undelivered
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. The dead keep calling, each with a message for someone still living: a widow's apology, a boy's warning about the river gate, a father's confession. Mara realizes the pattern — every caller died having left something unsaid. The bell rings again, twice now. Emotional beat: reluctant purpose replacing fear as she writes the messages down.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Knew
chapters.summary: POV: Mara, with flashbacks in her grandmother Ruth's voice via tape recordings. Ruth hosted the same show in the 1960s and heard the same voices; her journals reveal the bell counts toward one hundred, and that the founding families of Coldharbour once silenced a dying woman's plea. Emotional beat: shame and kinship — Mara inherits not just the gift but the debt.

chapters.title: The Skeptic's Wife
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Mara and Tom Ashford, whose wife Dora died last week and who refuses to hear 'her' message, calling Mara a vulture preying on grief. His teenage daughter secretly listens anyway. Meanwhile the bell rings four times in an hour. Emotional beat: love curdling into denial; the cost of refusing to listen.

chapters.title: Nineteen Eleven
chapters.summary: POV: Mara, interwoven with a found diary from 1911. The parishioners melted the bell to fund a war memorial, drowning out the sexton's daughter, who rang it nightly for her drowned mother and died unheard. Her unfinished hymn is what the dead are humming between calls. Emotional beat: horror rooted in communal guilt; the village's original sin surfaces.

chapters.title: The Count Accelerates
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. The bell rings in clusters — eleven, then nineteen. Power fails; only battery radios work, and every one of them picks up her frequency without being tuned. Half the village gathers at the station demanding answers; Tom arrives with a shotgun. Emotional beat: siege mentality, community fracturing under pressure as time visibly runs out.

chapters.title: Every Voice Answered
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. Mara broadcasts live, delivering each message on air while families listen in cars and doorways. Forgiveness lands unevenly — some weep, some rage — but each delivered message quiets one voice forever. Tom finally hears Dora say goodbye and collapses into his daughter's arms. Emotional beat: catharsis through listening; love against duty fulfilled one call at a time.

chapters.title: The Ninety-Ninth Ring
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. One message remains, and it's hers — from Ruth, recorded decades ago, telling Mara she was right to stop believing, wrong to stop listening. The bell begins its final swing. Mara understands the count can't be stopped, only answered, and takes the call live with the whole village holding its breath. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into acceptance at the threshold.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV: Mara. Mara speaks her answer aloud — 'I hear you' — and the bell stops at ninety-nine, cracked by nothing visible. The dead go quiet; the tower stands empty and stays empty. Weeks later, Mara keeps the show, taking ordinary calls from the living, leaving one line open always. Emotional beat: quiet resolution, grief integrated, the inheritance transformed from curse to covenant.
